# Affine-threshold approximate pair covers over the actual lattice

This note proves a quantitative local-to-global covering theorem. It uses
actual cap intersections, Brunn--Minkowski on continuous sections, and the
occupied-parity Helly theorem. It does not assert that every small-cap cover
satisfies its quantitative premise.

The underlying convex-root-threshold mechanism is already proved for
single-cap complements in Sections 1 and 5 of
`candidate af89470c3209e9d8`; its Section 6 also
already gives an exact obstruction to relative-volume superlevels. This
note extends that mechanism to residuals after unions of up to t original
caps and obtains a selected set of at most kt ORIGINAL caps with a
pointwise approximate-cover guarantee. The residual optimization programs
below are additional finite certificates. The convex-threshold idea itself
is not counted as a new mechanism.

## 1. Statement

Let C be a convex body in R^n x R^d, where d>=1. For each integer z let
K_z={x:(z,x) in C}. Suppose the full mixed volume

    M=sum_(z in Z^n) vol_d(K_z)

is positive. Let P be the finite set of integer bases with positive volume,
put V_z=vol_d(K_z), and let k be the number of parity classes occupied by
P, so k<=2^n. Let H_1,...,H_N be finitely many closed ambient halfspaces.

Let ell be an affine function on aff(P), nonnegative on conv(P). Suppose
that for every z in P there is a set J_z of at most two cap indices with

    vol_d(K_z minus union_(j in J_z) (H_j)_z) <= ell(z)^d.       (1)

Then there is a set I of at most 2k original cap indices such that

    mu(S minus union_(i in I) H_i) <= sum_(z in P) ell(z)^d.     (2)

Here mu is full mixed d-volume and S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d). Fibers of
zero d-volume do not affect either side. All inequalities concern the
actual closed caps and their actual open complements; vertical caps and
positive boundary mass are included without modification.

In particular, if every original cap has mixed mass at most B, then

    2k B >= M-sum_(z in P) ell(z)^d.                          (3)

Thus the condition

    sum_(z in P) ell(z)^d <= (1-2 gamma_d) M,
    gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d,                                    (4)

implies B>=gamma_d M/k. For d=1 the right side of (4) is zero, recovering
only the exact pair-cover case. For every d>=2 it is positive; for d=2
the permitted error is exactly M/9.

## 2. Convex uncovered-volume superlevels

For any set J of at most two cap indices define the actual convex set

    U_J=C intersect intersection_(j in J) H_j^c,

and its section volume

    f_J(z)=vol_d((U_J)_z).

The complements H_j^c are open halfspaces. Accordingly U_J need not be
closed, but it is bounded, convex, and measurable. This is sufficient for
Brunn--Minkowski. Set

    E_J={z in conv(P): f_J(z)^(1/d)>ell(z)}.

The set E_J is convex. Indeed, if p,q belong to E_J then their section
volumes are positive because ell is nonnegative. Convexity of U_J gives

    (1-t)(U_J)_p+t(U_J)_q subset (U_J)_((1-t)p+tq).

Brunn--Minkowski and the strict endpoint inequalities yield, for 0<t<1,

    f_J((1-t)p+tq)^(1/d)
       >=(1-t) f_J(p)^(1/d)+t f_J(q)^(1/d)
       >(1-t)ell(p)+t ell(q)=ell((1-t)p+tq).

This proves convexity directly, including empty or zero-volume sections
outside E_J. No unjustified concavity of a zero extension is used. Nor is
a relative-volume set {f_J/V_z>constant} asserted to be convex.

## 3. The occupied-parity Helly step and coverage

The positive base set P has the same-parity midpoint property: if p,q in P
have the same parity, their integer midpoint belongs to P. The Minkowski
inclusion of their positive full-dimensional fibers and Brunn--Minkowski
give positive volume at that midpoint. Thus the finite occupied-parity
Helly theorem from
`candidate 58dcf29bfb78a573`
applies to P and arbitrary convex sets, including the possibly nonclosed
sets E_J by the following explicit trace reduction. Replace each E_J by
the finite polytope conv(E_J intersect P). This polytope is contained in
E_J by convexity and has exactly the same trace on P. If a trace is empty,
that one set already supplies the desired subfamily. Otherwise apply the
finite polytope version of the cited theorem to these hulls, and transfer
its conclusion back by their identical traces. Thus no closedness of E_J
is assumed. The cited theorem has a self-contained finite separating-cap
proof; it needs only the stated midpoint property and k occupied labels,
rather than lattice completeness of P after zero-volume fibers are removed.

Hypothesis (1) says that every z in P is missing from at least one E_J.
Therefore the intersection of all these finitely many E_J misses P.
The parity Helly theorem selects m<=k of them, say E_(J_1),...,E_(J_m),
whose intersection also misses P. If P is already missed by a single
empty set, it is included in this statement. Set I=J_1 union ... union J_m.
Then |I|<=2k.

For every z in P, at least one selected E_(J_a) does not contain z, so
f_(J_a)(z)<=ell(z)^d. The part left uncovered by all the caps indexed by I
is contained in (U_(J_a))_z. Its volume is consequently at most ell(z)^d.
Summing over the finite positive base set proves (2).

The mass captured by the selected union is at least the right side of (3)
and at most the sum of at most 2k original cap masses. This proves (3)
and then (4). The proof never replaces a closed halfspace with an open one
of supposedly equal mixed mass: it uses the exact set-theoretic open
complement throughout.

## 4. Relative errors and an attained affine-majorant factor

Define the following explicit finite convex optimization quantity:

    A(P,V)=(1/M) min_L sum_(z in P) L(z)^d,

where L ranges over affine functions on aff(P) satisfying
L(z)>=V_z^(1/d) for every z in P. Such functions exist, for example the
constant max_z V_z^(1/d). The minimum is attained. To see this without
an unjustified coefficient compactness claim, identify affine functions
with their vectors of values on P. These vectors form a closed finite
dimensional linear subspace of R^P. The lower constraints are closed and
strictly positive in every coordinate. A bounded objective sublevel bounds
every coordinate above; hence it is compact and the continuous objective
attains its minimum. For d>1 its value vector is unique by strict convexity,
although uniqueness is unnecessary here.

The immediate exact bounds are

    1<=A(P,V)<=|P| max_z V_z/M.                            (5)

If the volume roots V_z^(1/d) are affine on P, in particular if all fiber
volumes are equal, then A(P,V)=1.

Suppose now that at each positive base some two original caps leave at
most tau V_z uncovered, for a fixed tau>=0. If L is an attained minimizer
above, put ell=tau^(1/d)L (ell=0 when tau=0). Then (1) holds and

    sum_z ell(z)^d=tau A(P,V) M.

Consequently

    B >= [1-tau A(P,V)] M/(2k).                           (6)

In particular the explicit sufficient condition

    tau A(P,V)<=1-2 gamma_d                              (7)

gives the sharp desired cap-cover budget B>=gamma_d M/k.

For equal-volume planar fibers, (7) is simply tau<=1/9. This assertion
has no restriction on n, the number of positive fibers, the directions
of the ambient halfspaces, or the directions of their integer components.
It is a sufficient covering theorem, not a claim that all bad caps have
such a pair at every fiber.
The equal-volume OC cap bound is already proved without this small-residual
hypothesis in Section 4 of `candidate af89470c3209e9d8`.
The displayed equal-volume threshold illustrates the new approximate-cover
certificate rather than claiming a newly solved OC class.

## 5. Interface with the three-cap small-minimum alternative

Suppose each positive fiber is owned by a group of three original caps
which cover it. Omitting a cap of minimum local area leaves uncovered area
at most that omitted cap's area. Therefore, if at every owned fiber

    min_j A_j(z)<=tau V_z,

the relative pair-cover hypothesis of Section 4 holds for the original
global cap family. Under (7), that case is already sufficient for the
sharp cap-budget conclusion, independently of the number of groups.

The small-cap-fiber quantity W_tau in
`candidate 40c46f71889ea6fc` measures only
part of the total mass; it does not automatically give this hypothesis
at every positive base. Nor is A(P,V) universally equal to one. These are
explicit remaining limitations, not omitted steps. This theorem gives a
quantitative use of the small-cap alternative when its stated global
threshold premise can actually be verified.

The count k throughout this note is the number of occupied parity classes.
The number m<=k in Section 3 is the number of selected uncovered-volume
superlevel sets. They are distinct quantities; no saturated-group
assumption is made.

## 7. Intrinsic measure, t-cap covers, and convex thresholds

The following is the more general theorem; Sections 1--6 are special cases.
Let C be any convex body in R^n x R^d with nonempty
S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d). Suppose q=dim_H(S)>=1, put

    V_z=H_q(C_z),
    P={z in Z^n: V_z>0},
    M=H_q(S)=sum_(z in P) V_z,

and let k be the number of occupied parity classes of P. Let t>=1 be an
integer and let ell:conv(P)->[0,infinity) be any finite convex function,
not necessarily affine. If at each z in P some at most t original closed
caps leave residual q-measure at most ell(z)^q, then at most kt original
caps leave, on EVERY positive integer fiber, residual measure at most
ell(z)^q. In particular they leave total residual at most sum_z ell(z)^q.

All quantities in this statement are well-defined. Each integer fiber is
compact and convex, so its Hausdorff dimension equals its affine dimension.
There are finitely many nonempty integer fibers; thus q is the largest of
their affine dimensions. Fibers of dimension q have positive finite H_q,
and all other integer fibers have H_q=0. The finite disjoint Borel fiber
union gives the displayed measure-sum identity and 0<M<infinity. The
standard normalization of H_q agrees with Euclidean q-volume on each
q-dimensional affine plane.

The new point in the proof is that real-base residual sections may have
dimension greater than q, and their H_q is then infinity. For a subset J
of at most t caps, retain the actual convex residual set

    U_J=C intersect intersection_(j in J) H_j^c,
    f_J(z)=H_q((U_J)_z) in [0,infinity],
    E_J={z in conv(P): f_J(z)>ell(z)^q}.

These E_J are convex, including the infinite-measure possibilities.
To verify this rigorously, let p,q_0 be two points of E_J and 0<s<1.
Their residual sections have positive H_q and hence affine dimension at
least q. A bounded convex set, closed or not, has nonempty relative
interior in its affine hull. It has positive finite H_q if that dimension
is q, and infinite H_q if its dimension is greater than q.

If either endpoint section has dimension greater than q, its Minkowski
average with any nonempty other section has dimension greater than q.
If both have dimension q but their direction spaces differ, the average
again has dimension greater than q: the sum of the two direction spaces
has dimension greater than q, and sums of relative open subsets fill a
relative open subset of that sum. Convexity places this average inside
the intermediate residual section. In these cases f_J at the intermediate
point is infinite, and that point belongs to E_J because ell is finite.

In the remaining case, both endpoint sections have the same q-dimensional
direction space. Translate them to that common Euclidean q-space and apply
ordinary Brunn--Minkowski to the measurable convex sets. Convexity of U_J
and of ell give

    f_J((1-s)p+s q_0)^(1/q)
      >=(1-s)f_J(p)^(1/q)+s f_J(q_0)^(1/q)
      >(1-s)ell(p)+s ell(q_0)
      >=ell((1-s)p+s q_0).

This proves convexity of E_J in every case. Nonclosed residuals cause no
failure: their relative interiors give the dimension assertions, and
Brunn--Minkowski holds for these bounded measurable convex sets. Empty or
lower-dimensional residual sections never appear as endpoints in this
argument, since membership in E_J forces positive H_q.

The positive integer base set P has the same-parity midpoint property.
Indeed the Minkowski average of two positive q-dimensional integer fibers
at a same-parity pair lies in their integer midpoint fiber and has
dimension at least q. It cannot have dimension greater than q, by the
definition of q over all integer fibers. Consequently that fiber has
positive H_q and its base belongs to P. This is exactly the property
needed by the finite occupied-parity Helly theorem; no common direction
space across different parity classes is assumed.

Apply that theorem to the finitely many E_J as in Section 3. The selected
at most k subsets J have union of cardinality at most kt. At each z in P,
one selected E_J misses z, so its actual residual has H_q at most ell(z)^q;
the residual left by the union is contained in it. This proves the stated
pointwise and total conclusions. Open complements and any full fiber
boundary masses have remained exact throughout.

If all cap masses are at most B, the resulting general budget is

    kt B >= M-sum_z ell(z)^q.                             (8)

For any target constant g with 0<=tg<=1, the condition
sum_z ell(z)^q<=(1-tg)M implies B>=gM/k. One may take g=gamma_d,
the ambient OC factor, or the stronger g=gamma_q when the error allowance
is nonnegative. Since k<=2^n, either gives the corresponding original
parity-budget conclusion. This remains a sufficient cap-cover theorem,
not a claim that every cap cover has such residual thresholds.

The affine-majorant factor in Section 4 extends verbatim with q in place
of d and intrinsic weights V_z. Its attainment and its exact value one
for affine volume roots remain unchanged.

## 8. Convex hinge thresholds and an attained residual program

Convexity in Section 7 permits ell=max{0,L} for an arbitrary affine
function L on aff(P). In particular L may be negative at bases where the
best local residual is zero; no artificial nonnegative constraint on L
is imposed there.

For the finite original cap family and a fixed t, define the actual
sampled residual roots

    e_z=min_{J: |J|<=t} H_q((U_J)_z)^(1/q),    z in P.

These are finite and the minimum is attained because the cap family is
finite and each actual integer section has finite H_q. A hinge threshold
ell=(L)_+ dominates e_z exactly when

    L(z)>=e_z on the subset where e_z>0;

the zero-residual bases impose no constraint on L. Thus the convex finite
optimization problem

    R_t=min_L sum_(z in P) (max{0,L(z)})^q
         subject to L(z)>=e_z whenever e_z>0              (9)

has an attained minimum. To check attainment without assuming bounded
affine coefficients, introduce variables T_z and write the polyhedral
constraints

    T_z>=0,    T_z>=L(z),
    L(z)>=e_z for each positive-residual z.

The projection of this polyhedron to the T coordinates is a closed
polyhedron. This elementary projection fact follows by eliminating one
affine variable at a time: each lower bound must be at most each upper
bound, while a missing one-sided family imposes no additional condition;
all resulting inequalities are non-strict linear inequalities. The
projected feasible set is nonempty, since a sufficiently large constant
L is feasible. The objective sum T_z^q has compact bounded sublevels on
the nonnegative orthant, so it attains its minimum on that closed feasible
set. A minimizing T has an associated affine L by feasibility; replacing
T_z by max{0,L(z)} can only decrease the objective and preserves all
constraints. Therefore this L attains (9).

Apply Section 7 with the attained hinge. At most kt original caps leave
total residual at most R_t. Consequently

    kt B >= M-R_t.                                       (10)

For example, in the planar t=2 case, the explicit condition R_2<=M/9
is enough for the sharp gamma_2/k cap budget. The program is a sufficient
certificate using actual cap residuals; there is no assertion that its
optimal value always satisfies M/9. If every e_z=0 then L=0 gives R_t=0,
recovering the exact local-to-global theorem.

## 9. The separate counting case q=0

No zero-th root or 0^0 is used. If q=0, every nonempty integer fiber is a
single point, and H_0 is counting measure. An exact local t-cap cover of
each point gives a global kt-cap cover by the original projection version
of the parity-Helly argument, using the convex sets proj(U_J) instead of
volume superlevels. In fact any covering family supplies a one-cap local
cover at each point, so at most k of the original caps cover the whole
finite S. This is the usual counting cap-budget bound M/k. Approximate
positive-power thresholds in Sections 7--8 are not invoked for q=0.
